summary: Specifies how Unicode can be used within MIME so email can carry text from many languages. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1641 describes how MIME can carry Unicode 1.1 text. It names the character set and specifies the order of the two octets used for each character.

questions: how to send unicode in email
how is unicode encoded in mime
subtitle: How to identify and encode Unicode 1.1 text in MIME messages.

tldr.problem: The RFC says Internet mail supported only 7-bit US ASCII, while MIME did not define Unicode as a permitted character set or specify its encoding.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the MIME charset name UNICODE-1-1 and represents each 16-bit character as two octets, with the more significant octet first.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1641 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. It directs mostly-ASCII text to a separate UTF-7 specification.

today: RFC 1641 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. The RFC metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Unicode in MIME
sections.content:
The memo describes Unicode 1.1 as a 16-bit character set covering most of the world's writing systems. Internet mail as defined by RFC 822 supported only 7-bit US ASCII. MIME could carry different character sets, but its specifications did not define Unicode or its encoding.

The RFC says that text which can be represented using US ASCII or ISO-8859 character sets should use those where possible. For text that is mostly ASCII with occasional other characters, it points to the separate UTF-7 memo.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME needed a defined way to identify Unicode text and encode it for email. The RFC also recommends using a smaller character set when it can represent the text.

sections.title: Unicode Characters as Octets
sections.content:
The specified Unicode character set is Unicode 1.1, with the character repertoire and coding of ISO/IEC 10646-1:1993 in UCS-2 form. Each 16-bit character is serialized as two octets, with the most significant octet first.

Text with an odd number of octets is ill-formed. The memo identifies the MIME charset as UNICODE-1-1 and says Binary or Base64 transfer encoding would normally be used for message bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each character uses two octets, sent most-significant octet first. A text body with an odd number of octets does not fit this encoding.

sections.title: Naming Unicode Versions
sections.content:
The memo sets a naming pattern for MIME charset registrations of Unicode versions and variants: UNICODE-major-minor or UNICODE-major-minor-variant. The major and minor parts are decimal digits that identify the Unicode version.

To improve interoperability, the RFC says to use the lowest version that can represent the text. Without a variant suffix, the name means the basic two-octet Unicode form. The memo gives UNICODE-1-1 as the lowest acceptable version name.
sections.plainLanguage: The charset name states which Unicode version is used and may also state a variant encoding. Senders should choose the oldest version that supports the text.

sections.title: MIME Examples and Security Note
sections.content:
The RFC shows two MIME text examples labelled charset=UNICODE-1-1 and encoded with Base64. One example carries Japanese characters; another carries a sequence containing a letter, a not-equal sign, a Greek letter and a full stop.

The Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show Unicode text inside Base64-encoded MIME parts. The memo does not discuss security issues.
